items.title: Get It? Can the sound from a battery-powered speaker carry more energy than the energy the battery supplies?

answer.html: No. By the law of conservation of energy, the speaker can only transform energy that the battery supplies; the sound's energy (plus the thermal energy produced) can at most equal the energy taken from the battery. In fact, some energy always becomes thermal energy, so the sound carries less than the battery's energy.

items.title: Figure 22, Predict: If the ball were thrown downward from the release point instead of simply dropped, what would its energy graph look like?

answer.html: The ball would begin with kinetic energy (and, at the release height, its full GPE), so the total mechanical energy bar would be larger than for the dropped ball. As it falls, the GPE bar shrinks and the KE bar grows by the same amount. The total mechanical-energy bar stays the same height at every point (conserved), but it starts with a nonzero KE bar.

items.title: CCC (Systems and System Models): Why is a model of a thrown baseball that ignores air resistance limited?

answer.html: The model assumes only gravity acts (no air resistance, a perfectly isolated ball-Earth system), so it predicts a symmetric arc and no loss of mechanical energy. In real life a fast baseball loses energy to air drag (thermal energy and sound), so it lands shorter than predicted, and a light ball such as a foam ball is affected much more. To present: state the assumptions, give the prediction (𝐾𝐸+ 𝐺𝑃𝐸 constant), then show real evidence (different ranges for a baseball and a foam ball launched alike) that the model leaves out other energy transfers. The model is a good approximation for dense objects over short distances.

items.title: Get It? A block starts at rest on a ramp where its GPE is 35.0 J relative to the bottom of the ramp. If friction transforms some of the system's energy, how does the block's kinetic energy at the bottom compare with 35.0 J?

answer.html: The final kinetic energy would be less than 35.0 J. Friction does negative work, transforming part of the initial gravitational potential energy into thermal energy, so 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝐺𝑃𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>−𝐸<sub>thermal</sub> < 35.0 J.

items.title: Get It? When a tennis ball hits the floor and most of its KE becomes elastic PE, what happens to the rest of the energy?

answer.html: The remainder is transformed into other forms: thermal energy (the ball and floor warm slightly because of internal friction as the ball deforms), sound (the "pop" of the bounce), and energy lost to air resistance. That is why each bounce is lower.

items.title: CCC (Energy and Matter): A pendulum bob swings back and forth. Explain how it provides evidence for conservation of energy.

answer.html: At the top of each swing the bob is momentarily at rest and has gravitational potential energy 𝑚𝑔ℎ (relative to the lowest point). As it swings down, GPE decreases while KE increases by the same amount, so at the bottom the speed matches the prediction from <sub>12</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> = 𝑚𝑔ℎ. On the way up KE turns back into GPE and the bob reaches nearly the same height it started from, showing that the energy is just changing form. The amplitude shrinks only slowly, because a small amount is lost as thermal energy and sound.

items.title: Practice Problems after Example Problem 5 (conservation of mechanical energy) Problem 1. A 62.0-kg skateboarder (with board) coasts at 6.4 m/s toward a smooth ramp and rolls up it until stopping momentarily. Find the initial kinetic energy, the height reached, and name the system.

body.html: 𝑚= 62.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 6.4 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 0 at the top; find 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub> and the height ℎ.

Choose the system skateboarder + board + Earth. If friction is negligible, no external force does work, so mechanical energy is conserved: 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>+ 𝐺𝑃𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>+ 𝐺𝑃𝐸<sub>𝑓</sub>. With the reference level at the bottom, <sup>12</sup>𝑚𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>

answer.html: System: skateboarder, board, and Earth. 𝐾𝐸<sub>𝑖</sub>= 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> J; the skateboarder comes to rest at a height ℎ= 2.1 m.

items.title: 2. The skateboarder now keeps pushing off the ground with one foot while rolling up the ramp and gets higher than 2.1 m. In what system is energy conserved, and where did the extra mechanical energy come from?

answer.html: Energy is conserved in a larger system: skateboarder + board + Earth, with the skateboarder's body included. The board gained mechanical energy (KE and GPE) from the chemical energy stored in the skateboarder's body (food), which the leg muscles convert to work on the board. (Some chemical energy also becomes thermal energy.)

items.title: Figure 25, Explain: A ceramic mug is dropped on a tile floor and shatters. What happened to the energy?

items.title: Get It? Contrast a perfectly inelastic collision with an elastic collision, and give an example of each.

answer.html: Both conserve momentum in a closed, isolated system. In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is the same before and after (two steel balls bouncing apart, nearly). In a perfectly inelastic collision the objects stick together and the kinetic energy decreases the most, because part of it is transformed into thermal energy, sound and permanent deformation (a lump of clay hitting a wall and sticking, or a football tackle where the players move off together).

items.title: Lesson 3 Check Your Progress Problem 1. A bungee jumper steps off a platform and falls, and the cord stretches until the jumper stops momentarily at the lowest point. Draw energy bar diagrams for (a) the instant at the platform before stepping off and (b) the lowest point.

items.title: 2. How can chemical, thermal, and kinetic energy all be added together as a single total?

answer.html: Because energy changes from one form to another and moves between objects, but the total amount in a closed, isolated system stays constant. All forms are measured in the same unit, joules, and can be added to give one conserved total.

items.title: 3. A lump of clay hits a wall and sticks. Is the clay's kinetic energy conserved? Is its momentum?

answer.html: The clay's kinetic energy is not conserved: the clay deforms permanently, so this is an inelastic collision, and the kinetic energy is transformed into thermal energy, sound, and the work of deforming the clay. The clay's momentum is also not conserved by itself, because the wall exerts an external force on it (the wall and Earth take up the momentum). Total energy is still conserved.

items.title: Figure 25, Explain: What happened to the energy in the car crash?

answer.html: The cars' kinetic energy decreased. Most of it was transformed into other forms: work deforming (crumpling) the metal, thermal energy (warmer metal), sound (the crash noise), and sometimes light (sparks). The total energy is conserved, but it is no longer kinetic energy.

items.title: Get It? Compare and contrast elastic and inelastic collisions

answer.html: Both conserve momentum in a closed, isolated system. In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is the same before and after (no kinetic energy goes into thermal energy, sound or deformation). In an inelastic collision kinetic energy decreases, because part of it is transformed into thermal energy, sound and permanent deformation (greatest when the objects stick together, a perfectly inelastic collision).

items.title: 3b. What is conserved in each step, and why?

answer.html: Collision (dart sticks to target): momentum is conserved because the collision is very brief and the external horizontal forces (string tension is vertical) are negligible; mechanical energy is not conserved (perfectly inelastic collision, some becomes thermal energy). items.title: 2. Why is energy considered a single quantity?

answer.html: Because energy changes from one form to another (kinetic, potential, thermal, etc.) and moves between objects, but the total amount in a closed, isolated system stays constant. All forms are measured in the same unit, joules, and can be added to give one conserved total.

items.title: 3. Gum and a rubber ball collide head-on and rebound: is KE conserved?

answer.html: No. Gum is soft and deforms permanently, so this is an inelastic collision. The kinetic energy decreases; the difference is transformed into thermal energy, sound, and the work of deforming the gum. Total energy is still conserved.

items.title: 4. Ball dropped from 8.0 m loses 1/5 of its mechanical energy at each bounce: how many bounces to reach about 4 m?

body.html: Each bounce leaves 4/5 of the mechanical energy, so the rebound height is also multiplied by 0.80 each time (𝑀𝐸∝ℎ).
After 3 bounces: 8.0(0.80)<sup>3</sup> = 4.1 m; after 4 bounces: 3.3 m.

answer.html: About 3 bounces (it rebounds to about 4.1 m after the third bounce, and falls below 4 m on the fourth)

items.title: 6. A device that delivers ten times more energy than is put in

answer.html: It cannot work. The law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be created, so the output energy can never exceed the input energy (and real devices always output less because some energy becomes thermal energy).

items.title: 7. A ball dropped 20 m: at half the fall time, is the PE more than, less than, or exactly half of the energy?

body.html: Falling from rest, distance 𝑑=<sub> </sub><sub>12</sub>𝑔𝑡<sup>2</sup>, so after half the total time the ball has fallen only <sub>14</sub> of the distance, not half.
Fallen = 20 / 4 = 5 m, so the height above the ground is 15 m and 𝑃𝐸= 𝑚𝑔(15) is 15 / 20 = 75% of the total.

answer.html: More than half: 75% of the energy is still potential energy (and 25% is kinetic) at half the fall time. The ball is slow at first, so it has not yet lost much height.
